name_en: Shu Pu-erh Tuo and Mini Tuo
origin_region: Yunnan · Dali and Kunming factories (leaf from Lincang and Pu'er)
processing: Wet-piled, dried and graded ripe leaf is steamed and machine-pressed into bowl-shaped nests: 100 g and 250 g tuo from the Dali factories, and 3–6 g individually wrapped mini tuo made from lower grades and fragments, sometimes with glutinous-rice herb added for scent.
harvest_season: Blended from any season; sold by production year.
appearance_dry: A hard dark-brown nest with a dimple underneath; mini tuo are marble-sized and foil-wrapped, big tuo have a smooth domed face with a few golden buds.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, cloudy on the first steep of a mini tuo, clearing after the rinse.
appearance_wet: Small chopped brown leaves and fragments that loosen slowly from the dense core.
taste_profile: Earthy-sweet and straightforward: dates, damp wood, a hint of cocoa, a medium body and a short clean finish; the Dali 100 g tuo add a dry, slightly smoky edge, and the mini tuo are rougher and dustier.

brewing.notes: Rinse twice with boiling water, the second rinse 20–30 seconds, to break the compression. For a mini tuo use one piece per 120–150 ml and give the first proper steep 30 seconds; for a big tuo break it from the dimple with a pick. Boiling water throughout.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and format: the Xiaguan 100 g ripe tuo made for export to France since the 1970s (the Xiao Fa tuo, 'sold-to-France tuo') is the classic and its 1990s and 2000s batches are an affordable aged ripe, while mini tuo are sold by count in tins and gift boxes with a year that is best read as a freshness date. Most ripe tuo on sale are 1–10 years old; tight pressing means they lose their pile smell slowly, so 3–5 years is a comfortable minimum for the big tuo, and mini tuo are drunk young and never cellared. Storage follows the usual pattern, with Guangdong-stored tuo softer and darker than Kunming-dry ones.
description:
Ripe tuo are shu pu-erh pressed into the nest shape that Dali made famous, and they come in two very different sizes: the 100 g and 250 g factory tuo, above all Xiaguan's Xiao Fa tuo, which has been shipped to France since the 1970s and sold there as a digestive health tea, and the 3–6 g mini tuo that fill supermarket tins and hotel drawers across China.

The big tuo are made from graded ripe leaf blended by the factory, steamed and pressed very hard; the Xiaguan version has a dry, faintly smoky house character on top of the usual ripe sweetness. Mini tuo are pressed by machine from lower grades and fragments, wrapped one by one, and quite often scented with the 'glutinous rice' herb that gives the popular nuomixiang mini tuo their sticky-rice aroma.

In the cup, a big ripe tuo with a few years on it is earthy-sweet, woody and comfortable, with a short clean finish; a mini tuo is the same idea coarser and dustier, and the first steep is usually cloudy. Both need two long boiling rinses and a patient first steep to open the compression, and both are happier in a big mug or pot than in a careful gongfu session.

They are sold by production year, the big tuo by the piece and the mini tuo by count, and prices are low. The Xiao Fa tuo is worth knowing as a budget aged ripe: its 1990s and 2000s batches are cheap and genuinely old. Mini tuo are convenience tea and should be judged as such; avoid any that smell of artificial flavouring through the wrapper, and expect the better ones to come from the established Dali and Kunming plants.

For travel, a handful of decent mini tuo in a bag does the job; for the table at home, one Xiao Fa tuo lasts a week.
sources_note: The Xiao Fa tuo export to France is generally dated to 1976 via the importer Fred Kempler; the 'glutinous rice' scent comes from the leaves of a Yunnan herb (Semnostachya menglaensis), not from rice. Card covers both the full-size ripe tuo and the mini tuo as requested.
